---
title: "Further Reading"
---

This book is deliberately short: it aims to give you the *machinery* for
deriving an objective, not to catalogue every objective in the literature.
These are the books and papers worth going to next.

## General textbooks covering this material in more depth

- Christopher Bishop, *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning*
  [@bishop2006prml] — Chapter 1 (probability and decision theory) and
  Chapter 4 (discriminative classification) cover much of Parts I–V of this
  book with more statistical machinery.
- Kevin Murphy, *Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction*
  [@murphy2022pmlbook] and *Advanced Topics* [@murphy2023pmladvanced] — the
  modern, exhaustive reference for everything probabilistic in this book,
  including proper scoring rules and calibration.
- Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, and Jerome Friedman, *The Elements of
  Statistical Learning* [@hastie2009elements] — the standard reference for
  regularization, model selection, and the statistical view of loss
  minimization.
- Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville, *Deep Learning*
  [@goodfellow2016deep] — Chapter 5 covers maximum likelihood estimation as
  the basis for essentially all deep learning objectives.

## Information theory

- Thomas Cover and Joy Thomas, *Elements of Information Theory*
  [@cover2006elements] — the canonical treatment of entropy, cross-entropy,
  and KL divergence, including the inequalities this book only states.
- Claude Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication"
  [@shannon1948mathematical] — where entropy, as used everywhere in this
  book, originates.

## Statistical decision theory and scoring rules

- Abraham Wald, "Statistical Decision Functions" [@wald1949statistical] and
  James Berger, *Statistical Decision Theory and Bayesian Analysis*
  [@berger1985statistical] — the formal decision-theoretic framework behind
  [Chapter 8](chapters/08-decision-theory-proper-scoring.qmd).
- Tilmann Gneiting and Adrian Raftery, "Strictly Proper Scoring Rules,
  Prediction, and Estimation" [@gneiting2007strictly] — the modern reference
  on proper scoring rules, well beyond what this book's single chapter
  covers.

## Statistical learning theory and surrogate losses

- Vladimir Vapnik, *Statistical Learning Theory* [@vapnik1998statistical] —
  the origin of the margin-based, empirical-risk-minimization view this book
  leans on throughout Parts V–VI.
- Peter Bartlett, Michael Jordan, and Jon McAuliffe, "Convexity,
  Classification, and Risk Bounds" [@bartlett2006convexity] — the precise
  theory of when a convex surrogate is statistically consistent for 0–1
  loss, referenced in [Chapter 9](chapters/09-surrogate-losses.qmd).

## Learning to rank

- Christopher Burges, "From RankNet to LambdaRank to LambdaMART: An
  Overview" [@burges2010ranknet] — a first-hand account of the reasoning
  behind [Chapters 11](chapters/11-ranknet.qmd) and
  [13](chapters/13-optimizing-ranking-metrics.qmd), by the author of both
  methods.
- Tie-Yan Liu's *Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval* survey and the
  original ListNet/ListMLE papers [@cao2007learning; @xia2008listwise] for
  the full pointwise/pairwise/listwise landscape this book only samples.

## Contrastive and representation learning

- Aäron van den Oord, Yazhe Li, and Oriol Vinyals, "Representation Learning
  with Contrastive Predictive Coding" [@oord2018representation] — the
  InfoNCE objective used throughout modern self-supervised learning.
- Ting Chen et al., "A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual
  Representations" (SimCLR) [@chen2020simple] for a concrete, influential
  application of the ideas in [Chapter 14](chapters/14-contrastive-objectives.qmd).

## Language models and preference optimization

- Ashish Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need" [@vaswani2017attention]
  — the architecture whose training objective is the subject of
  [Chapter 15](chapters/15-language-model-objectives.qmd).
- Rafael Rafailov et al., "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language
  Model is Secretly a Reward Model" [@rafailov2023direct] — the paper
  underlying [Chapter 16](chapters/16-preference-objectives.qmd); read it
  directly for the full derivation this book compresses.
- Paul Christiano et al., "Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human
  Preferences" [@christiano2017deep] and Long Ouyang et al., "Training
  Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback"
  [@ouyang2022training] for the RLHF lineage DPO grew out of.

## This author's other books

- [optimization-lab](https://github.com/ioannisantoniadis/optimization-lab)
  — for everything this book gestures at but doesn't derive about *how* a
  loss is actually minimized: convexity, conditioning, Gauss–Newton,
  high-dimensional loss landscapes.
- [modern-ai-systems-and-methods](https://github.com/ioannisantoniadis/modern-ai-systems-and-methods)
  — a broader field guide to where these objectives are used, in context,
  across supervised learning, ranking, generative models, and RL.
